groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
For a long time, many people assumed that bilingual speakers kept their two languages in separate mental boxes and simply opened one at a time. Recent research has shown that this picture is wrong. When bilinguals hear or read a word in one language, related words in their other language become active as well, even if that language is not being used.

This means that a bilingual brain is constantly managing competition. To speak in one language, it must select the right words and hold back those from the other. Some researchers believe that this daily practice strengthens general mental skills, such as focusing attention and switching between tasks. In several experiments, bilingual children and adults performed slightly better than monolinguals on tasks that required ignoring distracting information.

The evidence is not conclusive, however. Other studies, including some with very large groups of participants, have found no such advantage, and the debate continues. Managing two languages also has small costs. Bilinguals usually know fewer words in each language than people who speak only that language, and they more often feel that a word is "on the tip of the tongue." Most researchers agree that these costs are minor compared with the benefit of being able to communicate in two languages.

groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
Engineers facing a difficult problem sometimes look for an answer in an unexpected place: the natural world. This approach is known as biomimicry. Over millions of years, evolution has tested countless designs, and those that survive tend to be efficient. Rather than starting from nothing, a designer can study how a plant or animal has already solved a similar problem.

The best-known example is Velcro. In the 1940s, the Swiss engineer George de Mestral noticed that seeds stuck to his dog's fur after a walk. Under a microscope, he saw that each seed was covered with tiny hooks, and he copied the idea to create a new fastener. Decades later, engineers in Japan reshaped the nose of a high-speed train to resemble the beak of a kingfisher, a bird that dives into water with barely a splash. The redesigned train was quieter when it left tunnels and consumed less electricity.

Biomimicry is not a shortcut, however. Nature builds with materials and methods that factories cannot easily reproduce; spider silk, for instance, is remarkably strong for its weight, yet producing it in large quantities has proved difficult. Moreover, living things are shaped by the need to survive and reproduce, not to serve human purposes, so a natural design usually has to be adapted rather than simply copied.

listening.script: Today's story starts with a vegetable. I want to argue that the potato, yes, the ordinary potato, changed the history of Europe. Potatoes come from the Andes mountains of South America, where people had grown them for thousands of years. Spanish ships carried them to Europe in the fifteen hundreds. And at first? Almost nobody wanted them. They looked strange, they grew underground, and they belong to the same plant family as some poisonous species, so people didn't trust them. For a long time, in many places, potatoes were mostly fed to animals. So what changed people's minds? Hunger, mainly. A field of potatoes can feed far more people than the same field planted with wheat. Potatoes also grow in poor soil and in cool, wet weather, which describes a lot of northern Europe. And here's a detail I like. In wartime, soldiers could easily carry off the grain stored in a farmer's barn, but potatoes left in the ground were much harder to take. By the seventeen hundreds, rulers such as Frederick the Great of Prussia were actually ordering farmers to plant them. The result was a better-fed population that grew quickly, and many historians think that this growth supplied the workers for Europe's new factories and cities. Not bad for a vegetable nobody wanted.

options: How fish find food under the ice in winter
Why wax melts at a higher temperature than ice
How lakes in cold regions are formed
Why frozen water is less dense than liquid water
answers: Why frozen water is less dense than liquid water
questions.explanation: The professor asks why ice floats and explains it by the open pattern of molecules in ice, then shows why it matters.
questions.prompt: What is the main topic of the talk?

listening.script: Let's start with something you've all seen: ice cubes floating in a glass of water. It looks completely ordinary, right? But it's actually strange. With almost every other substance, the solid form is denser than the liquid, so the solid sinks. Drop a piece of solid wax into melted wax, and down it goes. So why is water different? It comes down to the shape of the water molecule and the way these molecules attract one another. In liquid water, the molecules are constantly moving, sliding past each other, and they can crowd fairly close together. But when water freezes, each molecule locks onto its neighbors in a fixed, open pattern, a bit like people holding hands at arm's length. That pattern has a lot of empty space in it. So the same amount of water takes up about nine percent more room as ice, which makes ice less dense than the water around it. Now, why should you care? Well, think about a lake in winter. Because ice floats, the lake freezes from the top down, and that layer of ice works like a blanket. The water underneath stays liquid, and fish survive until spring. If ice sank, lakes could freeze solid from the bottom up. Life in cold regions would look very different.

options: To describe a substance that never freezes
To show how most substances behave when they are solid
To explain what water molecules are made of
To give an example of a solid that floats
answers: To show how most substances behave when they are solid
questions.explanation: Wax illustrates the normal case: 'the solid form is denser than the liquid, so the solid sinks'. Solid wax goes down, so D is the opposite.

options: Why some products gain value as more people use them
How the telephone was invented and sold
Why new companies should charge low prices

answers: Why some products gain value as more people use them
higher.explanation: The professor defines a network effect, 'a product becomes more valuable to each user as the number of users grows', and gives two consequences.

listening.script: Suppose I gave you the only telephone in the world. What would it be worth to you? Nothing, obviously. There'd be nobody to call. Give a second person a phone, and yours suddenly has some value. Add a million people, and it becomes something you can hardly live without. Economists call this a network effect: a product becomes more valuable to each user as the number of users grows. Notice how odd that is. With most goods, it makes no difference to me how many other people own one. My umbrella keeps me just as dry whether or not you have an umbrella too. Now, network effects have a couple of consequences worth remembering. First, getting started is brutally hard. Nobody wants to join an empty network, which is why new platforms so often give their service away for free at the beginning. They're buying a crowd. Second, once a network gets big enough, it tends to pull ahead and stay ahead. A competitor might offer something technically superior and still fail, because what people are really paying for isn't the technology. It's access to everyone else. So when you hear that a market has ended up with one giant firm, don't assume the best product won. Sometimes it's simply the one that got big first.

options: Why the Iliad was finally written down
How modern readers should study Homer's language
How poets performed long poems without written texts
Why Balkan singers stopped performing heroic poems
answers: How poets performed long poems without written texts
higher.explanation: The professor asks how anyone remembered so long a poem and answers that singers composed as they sang, using ready-made phrases.
higher.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?

listening.script: The Iliad runs to more than fifteen thousand lines, and it took shape before the Greeks were widely using writing. So how on earth did anyone remember it? For a long time, the assumption was that poets simply had extraordinary memories and recited the poem word for word. Then, in the nineteen thirties, a young American scholar named Milman Parry tried something different. Instead of only studying old texts, he traveled to the Balkans, where singers still performed long heroic poems without being able to read, and he recorded them. What he found was that the singers weren't reciting from memory at all. They were composing as they sang. How? They'd absorbed a huge stock of ready-made phrases, each one shaped to fit the rhythm of a line. Think of Homer's 'swift-footed Achilles' or 'rosy-fingered dawn.' Readers today may find those repetitions tedious, but for the poet, they were building blocks. Whole scenes, like a feast, followed familiar patterns too. And here's the part I find most striking. The singers insisted that they sang a story exactly the same way every time. The recordings showed otherwise: no two performances matched. For them, 'the same' meant the same story, not the same words. So perhaps we should think of an epic less as a fixed text and more as a tradition of performances.

bullets: Explain the problem with your exam schedule.

questions.prompt: Write an email to Professor Whitfield. Write as much as you can and in complete sentences.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

Dear Professor Whitfield,

I am a student in your Introduction to Statistics class, and I am writing because I have a problem with the final exam schedule that was posted this morning. Your exam is on Thursday, December 17, at 9:00 a.m., and my World History exam is at exactly the same time in a different building.

Since I cannot attend both, I would like to suggest taking the statistics exam at another time. I am free on Thursday afternoon and all day Friday, and I would be happy to take it with another section or in your office, whichever is easier for you.

Could you please let me know what I need to do next? If there is a form to complete or an office I should contact, I will do so right away. I can also send you a copy of my schedule.

Thank you very much for your help.

Sincerely,
Camila Duarte

stages.title: Writing · Academic Discussion

groups.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
groups.instructions: Your professor is teaching a class on sociology. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

professor.name: Dr. Navarro
professor.post: This week we are examining how technology shapes relationships. Billions of people now use social media to share news, photos, and opinions with friends and strangers. Some researchers argue that these platforms strengthen our ties by keeping us in touch across long distances. Others claim that time spent online replaces deeper, face-to-face contact and leaves people lonelier. What is your view? Has social media made people more connected or more isolated, and why?

students.name: Thabo
students.post: I believe social media has made us more connected. My family lives in three different countries, and before these apps existed we spoke only a few times a year. Now we share photos and messages every day in a group chat. I know what my cousins are doing, and I feel much closer to them than my parents did to their relatives.

students.name: Elif
students.post: In my opinion, people are more isolated now. We may have hundreds of online friends, but most of those relationships are shallow. I often see groups of friends sitting together in a café while each person looks at a phone. Liking someone's photo takes one second, and it is not the same as really listening to them.

questions.prompt: Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

I think social media can do both, but in my experience it has made people more connected overall. Thabo's example of a family spread across several countries is convincing, and I would add another kind of connection that he did not mention: people with unusual interests or problems can now find others like them. A teenager in a small town who loves astronomy, or someone learning a rare language, used to have no one to talk to. Today such people can join online communities and feel that they belong somewhere. I understand Elif's point that many online friendships are shallow, and it is true that phones sometimes interrupt real conversations. However, that is a problem of how we use the technology, not of the technology itself. If people set limits, for example by putting their phones away during meals, they can enjoy both kinds of contact.

stages.instructions: 10 minutes. Write a post for the class discussion. Your response is saved for review; it is not scored automatically.

groups.title: Take an Interview
groups.instructions: You have agreed to take part in a research study about shopping habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

toefl.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about shopping habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 1 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: A few weeks ago, I bought a secondhand bicycle, and I am still very pleased with it. I had been taking the bus to the university every day, which was slow and cost me quite a lot each month. I found the bike on a website where students sell things they no longer need, and the price was less than half of what a new one costs. The owner let me ride it around the block before I paid, so I knew that the brakes and the gears worked well. Now I get to class in fifteen minutes, I save money, and I get some exercise at the same time. It was easily my best purchase this year.

listening.script: Thank you for joining me today. I'd like to begin with a recent experience. Please tell me about the last time you bought something that you were really pleased with. What was it, and why were you happy with it?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 2 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I prefer shopping online for most things, mainly because it saves time. I have classes all day and a part-time job in the evening, so I can't easily get to the stores before they close. Online, I can compare prices from several sellers in a few minutes and read what other buyers thought of the product. That said, there are some things I always buy in person. Shoes are a good example, because sizes differ so much between brands, and I also like to choose my own fruit and vegetables. So I would say I do about three-quarters of my shopping online and the rest in real stores.

listening.script: Some people enjoy going to stores in person, while others would rather buy almost everything online. Which do you prefer, and why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 3 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: Yes, I mostly agree. When people see a sign that says fifty percent off, they focus on how much they are saving rather than on how much they are spending. I have done this myself. Last winter I went into a store for a pair of gloves and came out with a jacket as well, only because it was on sale. I didn't really need it, and I have worn it twice. Sales also create a feeling of hurry, because the offer ends soon, so shoppers don't take time to think. Of course, a sale is useful if you were already planning to buy that item. The trick, I think, is to make a list first and keep to it.

listening.script: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people believe that discounts and sales encourage shoppers to spend more money than they had planned. Do you agree or disagree? Why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 4 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: Yes, I strongly believe schools should teach this. Managing money is a skill that everyone needs, but many young people only learn it by making expensive mistakes. When I first lived away from home, I spent most of my monthly budget in two weeks because nobody had shown me how to plan. A short course could cover simple things, such as writing a budget, comparing prices, and understanding how interest on a loan works. Some people argue that parents should teach these things, but not every parent has the time or the knowledge. If schools include this, every student gets the same chance to start adult life with good habits.

listening.script: Here is my last question. Do you think schools should teach students how to manage their money, for example how to plan a budget and compare prices? Why or why not?
